ENT CLINICAL NOTE  

Subjective:  
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: 5-day history of persistent dry cough and profuse nasal discharge; no clear trigger or exposure identified.  
- Symptom timeline and progression: Symptoms began ~5 days ago; cough occurs every 20–30 min; nasal discharge described as “constantly streaming,” now green in color; reports intermittent subjective fever (feels hot then chills) but has not taken a temperature. No reported worsening since onset.  
- ENT symptoms:  
  • Throat: dry sensation, soothed temporarily by hot lemon beverage; no throat-tightness, dysphagia, odynophagia, drooling, or voice change.  
  • Nose: continuous rhinorrhea (green), no epistaxis, no facial pain/pressure reported.  
  • Ears: denies ear pain.  
  • Airway/respiratory: no stridor, noisy breathing, or dyspnea.  
  • Swelling: denies lip, tongue, uvular, or facial swelling.  
  • Neck: no pain or swelling reported.  
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: None stated. No prior ED visits or injections for similar illness.  
- Allergies and current medications:  
  • Seasonal hay fever (pollen); no drug allergies reported.  
  • Metformin – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  • “Lisinopril 200” (likely mg; dose/frequency not clearly documented) – conflict noted with usual dosing ranges.  
  • Over-the-counter: Lemsip (contains paracetamol) 2–3 per day; occasional cough syrup at night – doses/frequency not documented.  
- Social context: Lives with partner and dog; employed as office manager; currently in a private setting for call.  

Objective:  
- Observable swelling: None reported or seen via video.  
- Airway/breathing: Patient denies shortness of breath; no stridor reported; voice sounds normal on call.  
- Mental status: Alert, oriented, conversant.  
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded (video consultation only).  
- Others present: None; patient alone during call.  

Assessment:  
- Probable acute viral upper respiratory infection (rhinopharyngitis) with post-nasal drip–related dry cough.  
  • Justification: 5-day duration, green nasal discharge, dry cough, absence of dyspnea/airway compromise, no focal ENT red-flag features; onset consistent with common viral illness.  
- Differential includes early bacterial rhinosinusitis or lower respiratory tract infection; monitor for evolving signs (persistent fever, purulent sputum, chest pain).  
- No evidence of allergic reaction or anaphylaxis.  
- Chronic conditions: Type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension (on metformin and lisinopril).  

Plan:  
- Symptomatic care: Continue Lemsip as needed but avoid other paracetamol-containing products; limit cough syrup to nighttime if sleep-disrupting.  
- Monitoring: Purchase a thermometer; check temperature twice daily.  
- Escalation criteria/red flags: Seek further medical review if any of the following occur:  
  • Temperature persistently ≥37.5–38 °C despite symptomatic care.  
  • Worsening or persistent fever beyond ~1 week.  
  • Increased cough frequency, production of purulent sputum, or hemoptysis.  
  • New or worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, or noisy breathing.  
  • Ear pain, severe sinus/facial pain, or swelling.  
- Follow-up: Re-contact primary care/ENT service or call emergency services if red flags develop; otherwise, expected recovery within 1–2 weeks, with cough possibly lasting longer.  
- Chronic disease advice: Maintain routine diabetes and blood-pressure follow-up; ensure availability of home blood glucose monitoring if recommended by GP.  
- Safety: Remain accompanied if feeling faint or unwell; ensure ability to access emergency services if needed.  

Quality checks (document_quality):  
● Missing but clinically expected elements: Objective vital signs (temperature, HR, BP, RR, SpO₂); physical examination of nasal mucosa, throat, lymph nodes, chest; confirmation of actual lisinopril dose and frequency; documented blood glucose readings; vaccination status (e.g., influenza, COVID-19).  
● Internal conflicts: Patient stated lisinopril dose as “200,” which is outside usual dosing range—conflict noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear overall; occasional inaudible gaps but did not affect extraction of main clinical information.
